summary: Describes NETCRT, a character display protocol, now revised after circulation at the May meeting. It was created because Rand wanted network access to URSA, UCLA CCN's display-based conversational remote job entry system, used to enter and edit programs and examine output.

plainLanguage.summary: NETCRT describes a virtual character display that lets a remote user interact with UCLA's URSA system. The server can control the screen buffer, move the cursor, write text and read selected text back.

questions: how does a virtual character display work
what commands can the virtual character display run
subtitle: A virtual character display protocol for remote use of UCLA's URSA system.

tldr.problem: UCLA's URSA remote job entry system required control of a character display that a simple typewriter-style terminal protocol could not provide.
tldr.mechanism: NETCRT models a virtual character display with a screen buffer, cursor, keyboard, commands and Local and Control states.
tldr.outcome: The specification describes how a remote host can exchange display commands and responses with URSA, while noting that implementation depended on an interested user site.

today: RFC 205 is a character display protocol specification published in August 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Why NETCRT Was Proposed
sections.content:
UCLA developed NETCRT to provide network access to URSA, its display-based conversational remote job entry system. URSA was designed for fast character displays with local buffers; its editor could not be used effectively from a typewriter-like console.

NETCRT defines a virtual character display (VCD) simulated by a process on the user's host. The document publishes the protocol to invite comments and because some features might help designs for full graphical displays.
sections.plainLanguage: URSA expected a screen that could update individual characters, so a simple text connection was not enough. NETCRT describes a screen that a remote computer can control through network messages.

sections.title: The Virtual Display and Its States
sections.content:
The VCD consists of a rectangular screen, a local character buffer, a cursor register, a keyboard and a communication interface. The server sends command segments and receives response segments containing status or text read from the buffer.

In Local state the keyboard is unlocked; in Control state it is locked while the server executes commands. Transmit or Break can put the VCD into Control, and Reset or a server LOCAL command can return it to Local. Break also sends an interrupt request.
sections.plainLanguage: The virtual display keeps a local copy of its screen text and a cursor position. It switches between user control and server control, so both sides can manage the display.

sections.title: Commands and Message Exchange
sections.content:
Commands include ERASE, BLANK, UNBLANK, LOCAL, cursor movement, FIND, SAVE, RESTORE, WRITE, READ, SREAD and AWRITE. Read commands return requested text and the cursor position. The server can choose which portions of the buffer to read.

For server-initiated breaks, the server sends an interrupt on the control connection and a SYNC command on the data connection. The VCD coordinates these signals so buffered commands do not prevent the server from regaining control.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can clear the display, move the cursor, write text or request text from the buffer. A synchronization command helps the server regain control when messages arrive at different times.
